div.p: Real-time systems interact with external environment and hence often have demanding performance requirements. Designing and developing complex realtime systems is a challenging task. Model based programming is a relatively new approach towards integrated system development that simplifies this task. Hard real-time requirements pose additional problem that the timing constraints imposed must be met, or else some catastrophic failure occurs. In this paper, we demonstrate that hard real-time requirements can be satisfied by a suitable scheduling scheme in model based programming environment. The scheduling scheme consists of a scheduling algorithm and schedulability tests. Both the scheduling algorithm and the schedulability tests can be performed in polynomial time, hence can be used in dynamic environment where on-line restructuring of the computation model may be necessary.

div.head: The Application Environment
div.p: The research in process control area at Vanderbilt University has led t o the development of Intelligent Process Control System (IPCS') [I] [2]. IPCS is a realtime supervisor for large scale industrial processes. It controls various activities, monitors different operations and with the sensory information from the plant, it is capable to diagnose a fault in the system [3], should one occur.

IPCS is a model based system. It incorporates the system information in the form of mathematical or physical models. These models are used for validation and interpretation of sensory information, tracking changes in the state of the plant, and even for the control of the reconfiguration of the processing system.
IPCS has been developed in the framework of Multigraph Architecture (MGA) [l]. It is a multilayer architecture as shown in Figure 1. The various layers are as follows.

0 Models and Model Builder. The top level of MGA-based system includes models. Models represent selected qualitative and quantitative information of both the environment (system to be controlled or monitored) and the control/monitoring system itself.
0 Model Interpreter. The models, as explained above, store the information in descriptive form.

In order to use this information for monitoring, controlling and diagnostics, these models must be transformed into an executable. The process that maps the models into executable computing structures is called Model Interpretation.

div.head: The Dynamic Reconfiguration in
div.p: An important capability offered by the Multi raph Architecture is its dynamic reconfigurability [47. In the Multigraph Architecture, the dynamic reconfiguration is not limited to adjustments in the parameters of the system. The architecture allows structural changes during run-time. At the execution level, the dynamic reconfiguration is manifested by the addition/deletion of nodes and edges in the graph and reconfiguration of the graph.
If the monitoring system senses some abnormal conditions, can it generate a shut down message within so much time?

To answer such questions calls for Hard Real-Time capabilities. Considering the possibility of run-time reconfiguration in the Multigraph Execution Environment, it is important to note that execution of the scheduling algorithm and the schedulability tests itself has timing constraints. This requires that these algorithms be fast (polynomial).

div.head: The Extended Deadline Monotonic Algorithm For the Graph Computation Model
div.p: It has been proved [5] that the Deadline Monotonic Algorithm is an optimal priority assignment algorithm for independent tasks, if the deadlines are less than or equal to the periods of the tasks. There is no optimality result (other than the exhaustive search) available for the case when deadlines can be greater than the periods of the tasks. For the interdependent tasks, as in our model, results are not available even for the case where deadlines are shorter than the periods. We have extended the Deadline Monotonic Algorithm for our graph computation model. Briefly, the algorithm is as follows. We start with the most stringent timing constraint. For each timing constraint, we choose a set of nodes in the graph that should be assigned a priority in order to help meet the timing constraint. While choosing this set, we take into account various dependencies between the nodes in the graph. Then, we assign the next highest priority t o those nodes in this set that have not already been assigned a priority. For more detailed description of the algorithm, please see [7].

div.head: The time complexity of this algorithm is polynomial ( O ( n 2 d ) ,
div.p: where n is the no. of nodes in the control graph and d is the number of timing constraints), and simulation studies show that its performance is close to the optimal.

div.head: Schedulability Analysis
div.p: Development of the Schedulability Tool involved three steps.
0 Identification of the necessary conditions. If these conditions can not be satisfied, then the timing constraints will not be met and further investigations are useless.
0 Derivation of the polynomial time schedulability conditions for independent tasks. 0 Extension of these schedulability condition for the graph computation model.

In the first steps, the schedulability tool tests some conditions that must be satisfied, in order to meet the timing constraints. A simple example of such conditions is checking of demanded processor utilization by all the nodes. If this demand exceeds unity, then the timing constraints will not be met, and it is not necessary to carry out remaining schedulability analysis.

For a set of independent tasks, if the deadlines are greater than the periods, then the only schedulability test available is due to Lehoczky [6]. However, this test does not lead t o a polynomial (in number of tasks) time algorithm. We have derived the sufficient condition to analyze schedulability of independent tasks. div.head: Simulation Studies
div.p: The extended deadline monotonic algorithm is based on heuristics. Hence, the performance of the overall scheduling scheme has been evaluated using simulations.

The Performance Measures: It must be noted that the scheduling scheme proposed operates in two phases. The first phase is to assign the priorities us- ing the extended deadline monotonic algorithm. The second phase is to check if the deadlines will be met with that priority assignment. Both the phases need a performance measure. The performance of the overall scheme is function of performances of both the phases. 0 The Performance Measure for the priority assignment algorithm: Zhao et. al. [lo] have defined success ratio of scheduling algorithms. This is a good performance measure for suboptimal scheduling algorithms. Given a scheduling problem, the schedule obtained by an optimal algorithm may or may not meet the deadlines. In a given problem space, assume that the optimal schedule meets deadlines N o number of times. Of that, a schedule obtained by a sub-optimal algorithm may successfully meet the deadlines N s number of times. Then, the success ratio of the sub-optimal algorithm is %.

0 The Performance Measure for the Guarantee Algorithm: Of those cases, in which the suboptimal algorithm actually finds a schedule that would meet the deadlines, the guarantee algorithm can guarantee only NG cases, where, NG 5 N s . The success ratio of the Guarantee algorithm is its performance measure, and is given by E.

0 The Performance measure of the Overall Scheme: Given a hard real-time scheduling problem, it is not enough to find a schedule. It is equally important t o guarantee that the schedule meets the timing constraints. The success radio of the overall scheme is then given by E.

The Simulation Setup: The purpose of the simulation studies is to evaluate the effectiveness of the extended deadline monotonic algorithm and the guarantee scheme separately in various cases. A possible approach to do this is as follows.
1. Take a graph scheduling problem that is known to be schedulable by priority assignment technique. That is, it is known that with some priority assignment scheme, all the deadlines are met.
Apply the extended deadline monotonic algorithm to assign priorities.
3. Simulate the system with these priorities. If the deadlines are met in this simulation, then the extended deadline monotonic algorithm has been successful in this case.
Apply the guarantee algorithm t o see if it guarantees the timing constraints with the priority assignments determined in step 2.

If the extended deadline monotonic algorithm has not been successful as tested in step 3, then the guarantee algorithm will not guarantee the deadlines. Note that the guarantee algorithm is successful in this case, but this case will not be taken into account for measuring its success, because the guarantee algorithm is not challenged. However, if the extended deadline monotonic algorithm was successful, then if the guarantee algorithm does guarantee the timing constraints, then the guarantee algorithm will be said to be successful.
6. If both the extended deadline monotonic algorithm and the guarantee algorithm are successful, then the overall scheme will be said to be successful.
Repeat steps 1 through 6 for various different problems, that are known to be schedulable by the priority assignment technique.

It turns out that finding a problem that is known to be schedulable is itself a difficult task. To find such a problem, one would have to come up with some arbitrary graph with arbitrary timing constraints. Then exhaustive search could be done to check if the problem is schedulable or not. The exhaustive search in this context would mean using all possible priority assignments one by one, and performing simulation for each of the assignment to check if the timing constraints are being met. It is easy to see that the number of possible priority assignments grows exponentially with the number of nodes in the graph. That makes this approach too time consuming. Hence, a different approach, which is described below, has been taken. Similar argument and approach can also be found in [lo].
First take a graph with nodes having given computation times. Choose timing constraint paths in the graph.
Assign priorities to the nodes arbitrarily.
Simulate the execution of the nodes in the graph, with the assigned priorities. Note the maximum times needed for data tokens to traverse the timing constraint paths.
A graph scheduling problem with (a) Given graph (b) Chosen timing constraint paths (c) The deadlines equal to the maximum traversal times found in step 3.
is known to be schedulable. A possible solution is the priority assignment done in step 2.
The simulation studies indicate that the performance of the overall scheduling scheme is 85%-90% of that of the optimal scheme.

The discussion here assumed that the processor was the only resource needed for the execution of the nodes. However, a node may need additional resources for its execution. These resources may be shared among many nodes in the graph, and they may be protected by semaphores for mutually exclusive access.

We have already done some preliminary work in this direction 91. We have shown that the Priority Ceiling Protocol Ill] or the Priority Limit Protocol [12] can easily be used as a resource access control policy over our base scheduling (the extended deadline monotonic scheduling) algorithm. The schedulability conditions developed for the base scheduling algorithm can also be easily modified.

Another research direction is to exploit the hierar- chical modeling in the Multigraph Architecture for the purpose of scheduling. The models in the Multigraph Architecture can be viewed as a tree, in which the root is a model that contains other models, these models, in turn, contain some other models and so on. The models at the lowest level (leaves in the tree) directly represent the control graph in the MEE. The models at the upper level can be thought of as macro-nodes in A Plan for Future Research a computation graph at a higher level. It is possible to start the scheduling algorithm at an upper level in the hierarchy, where the number of nodes are much smaller, and progressively use more refined graphs at lower levels, only if the schedule is not guaranteed at the upper level.
